title: Trump v. Illinois (2025)
summary: The President may federalize the National Guard under 10 U.S.C. § 12406(3) only when he is unable with the regular military to execute the laws, so a deployment justified by inherent authority to protect federal personnel and property, with no statute allowing the military to execute the laws, cannot be sustained on an application for a stay.
notes: Supreme Court of the United States, 2025. Key line: "So before the President can federalize the Guard under § 12406(3), he likely must have statutory or constitutional authority to execute the laws with the regular military and must be 'unable' with those forces to perform that function." (unsigned opinion of the Court)

sections.Parties: The applicant is the United States, acting for President Trump, the Secretary of War, and the federal immigration agencies operating in Chicago. The respondents are the State of Illinois and the other plaintiffs who sued to stop the deployment; the opinions name only Illinois. The State objected to the federalization and deployment of about 300 members of the Illinois National Guard and to the arrival of federalized Texas Guard members. The Government wanted the Guard free to protect an Immigration and Customs Enforcement processing facility in Broadview, Illinois, and federal officers working in and around Chicago. The dispute reached the Court on the Government's emergency application for a stay of the district court's order, not on certiorari.
sections.Material Facts: Crowds at the Broadview ICE facility, the only intake center for the Chicago area, blocked its gates, damaged the building, slashed tires on government vehicles, and once poured flour into a federal vehicle's gas tank. Some carried loaded guns and gas masks; more than 30 officers were injured. On October 4, 2025, ten civilian cars boxed in a Border Patrol vehicle and two rammed it; Chicago police dispatch recorded that no units would respond. That day the President invoked 10 U.S.C. § 12406(3), which lets him federalize the Guard when he is "unable with the regular forces to execute the laws of the United States," and called 300 Illinois Guard members into federal service to perform protective activities. The next day Texas Guard members were federalized and sent to Chicago. The Government relied on inherent constitutional authority to protect federal personnel and property, not on the Insurrection Act.
sections.Procedural History: Illinois sued in the Northern District of Illinois. The district court entered a temporary restraining order barring both the federalization and the deployment of the Guard in Illinois, reading "unable" as literally incapable and refusing deference to the President's determination. The Seventh Circuit denied a stay in relevant part: the Guard could remain federalized within Illinois, but the bar on deployment stayed in force. The Government applied to the Supreme Court for a stay. After the response and reply, Justice Barrett referred the application to the full Court. The Court then directed supplemental letter briefs on a question the district court had decided but the parties' briefs had not raised: what "regular forces" means. In the lower courts both sides had said it meant civilian federal law enforcement; in the supplemental briefs Illinois switched to the district court's view that it means the regular military. The Court denied the application on the emergency docket without oral argument.
sections.Issue: Whether the Government is entitled to a stay of the district court's order, which turns on whether the President likely had statutory authority under 10 U.S.C. § 12406(3) to call the Illinois National Guard into federal service. That question breaks into two parts the Court flagged for supplemental briefing: what the phrase "regular forces" refers to, the regular United States military or civilian federal law enforcement officers such as ICE and the Federal Protective Service; and whether the President is "unable with the regular forces to execute the laws of the United States" when the obstacle to using the military is that no statute or constitutional provision lets the military execute the laws at all. A further question, whether courts may review the President's findings under § 12406(3), was raised below but not decided.
sections.Holding: The application for a stay is denied. The Court concluded that "the term 'regular forces' in § 12406(3) likely refers to the regular forces of the United States military." Because the statute asks whether the President is unable with the military to execute the laws, "it likely applies only where the military could legally execute the laws," and under the Posse Comitatus Act those cases are exceptional. The Government identified no statute creating an exception and relied instead on inherent protective authority, which by the Executive Branch's own longstanding view is not "executing the laws." So, "at least in this posture, the Government has not carried its burden to show that § 12406(3) permits the President to federalize the Guard in the exercise of inherent authority to protect federal personnel and property in Illinois." The Court did not reach the reviewability of presidential findings.
sections.Reasoning: The opinion rests on statutory text read against a neighboring statute. Section 12406(3) conditions federalization on the President being "unable with the regular forces to execute the laws." Reading "regular forces" as the regular military, the Court held that the condition requires an assessment of the military's ability to execute the laws, which presupposes that the military lawfully could do so. The Posse Comitatus Act, 18 U.S.C. § 1385, forbids the military from executing the laws "except in cases and under circumstances expressly authorized by the Constitution or Act of Congress," so before invoking § 12406(3) the President likely must have some statutory or constitutional authority for the military to execute the laws and must then be unable with those forces to do so. The Government invoked no Posse Comitatus exception. It relied on inherent Article II authority to protect federal personnel and property, but it also maintained, consistent with the Executive Branch's long view, that protective functions are not "execut[ing] the laws" under the Posse Comitatus Act. Citing Azar v. Allina Health Services, the Court applied the presumption that Congress does not silently attach different meanings to the same term in related statutes: if protecting officers is not executing the laws for one statute, it is hard to see how it is for the other. The stay applicant bears the burden, the stage is preliminary, and the Court did not decide whether courts may review the President's findings.

topics.lrs-s-enabling-statute: The President's power to federalize the Guard exists only on the terms of § 12406(3), and the Court refused to let inherent Article II protective authority substitute for the statutory condition the Government could not satisfy.
topics.lrs-s-conditional-legislation: Section 12406(3) is conditional legislation triggered by a presidential finding of inability; the majority tested the legal premise of that finding while Alito, citing Martin v. Mott, argued the President's judgment of the exigency is conclusive.
topics.lrs-k-statutory-structure: The majority read "execute the laws" in § 12406(3) together with the Posse Comitatus Act and applied the presumption that the same phrase carries the same meaning in related statutes; Alito answered that the presumption is not conclusive.
topics.lrs-k-canons: The opinions clash over consistent-usage, the ordinary meaning of "unable" (literal incapacity, substantial impairment, or legal barrier), and whether the Court may add an unwritten condition to the enacted text.
topics.procedure: The case arrived on an emergency application to stay a temporary restraining order, referred by the Circuit Justice to the full Court, decided on supplemental letter briefs without argument, and framed throughout as likely conclusions at a preliminary stage.

learning.separateOpinions: The Court's unsigned opinion denied the stay; with Justice Kavanaugh concurring in the judgment and three Justices dissenting, the vote was 6 to 3. Kavanaugh agreed that "regular forces" likely means the military but would have denied the stay only because the President had not yet made the required determination that he is unable with the military, as distinct from civilian officers, to execute federal law; he warned that the Court's broader reading could bar federalizing the Guard to protect a besieged courthouse and would have called for more briefing or argument. Alito, joined by Thomas, dissented: the Court violated the party-presentation principle by reviving an argument respondents had waived three times, added words to the statute, misread the Posse Comitatus Act (which § 12406(3) itself satisfies as an Act of Congress), and ignored Martin v. Mott's rule that the President's judgment of the exigency is conclusive; on the parties' own premise the record of violence showed the President was "unable," meaning substantially impaired, and a stay should issue. Gorsuch dissented separately, urging caution, deciding only the preserved arguments, and agreeing with Parts I-A, B-1, C, and D of Alito's opinion that the declarations supported a stay.
learning.why: The case shows a court policing the statutory condition on a presidential power: even a broad grant to the President, triggered by his own finding, is read with its neighboring statutes and can fail on the emergency docket when the Government cannot name a lawful source for the underlying military role. The concurrence and dissents set out the competing positions on party presentation, deference to presidential fact-finding under Martin v. Mott, and how much an interim order should decide.
